messages.subject: pystan model parsing problems on OS X 10.9 / MacPorts py27
parts:
I'm posting this message before I go spend all day debugging this. On two different systems with OS X 10.9 and Python 2.7 installed via MacPorts (one is a "wide" build, one not), I get the following (a minimal testcase, but full models show either this or "Expected: model declaration"):


>>> from pystan._api import stanc
>>> result = stanc('parameters {real y;} model {y ~ normal(0,1);}', 'normal1')
>>> print result['msg']
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=1, column=46

parameters {real y;} model {y ~ normal(0,1);}
                                             ^-- here


DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Parser expecting: <model declaration>

Any ideas?

Thanks,
-Ken

If anyone has gotten PyStan working under OS X 10.9 (Mavericks), details would
be welcome...

-a

parts:
Ken & Allen,

On my system I was able to reproduce below error using command line stan and after installing pystan. The command line output on my machine is attached below and seems identical to what Ken got. 'simple_model.stan' basically contains Ken's 1-liner.

It's been a while since I used Python, but while running 'pip install pystan' I noticed several fragments like the one attached below. From this I'm assuming that the stanc compiler is build using optimization level -O3. The Stan parser (stanc) will fail when build with optimization level -O3 using clang++.

Over the summer I developed a fix (needed to enable c++11 extensions), but that (or a similar update) has not yet been merged into 2.0.1. 

As I said, my Python/Django days are a while ago, but I'm pretty sure if the stanc would be build with -O0 (like O_STANC = 0 in the vanilla makefile of the stan distribution) this will fix the issue.

Regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@icloud.com

> 1-liner.

> attached below. From this I'm assuming that the stanc compiler is build using optimization level -O3. The Stan parser
> (stanc) will fail when build with optimization level -O3 using clang++.

Right --- the problem is that the Boost lib we use
is very heavy on the template metaprogramming and lazy
eval, so it's very taxing on compilers. (We had the
opposite problem with Windows 32-bit, where it would only
build with -O3.)

> Over the summer I developed a fix (needed to enable c++11 extensions), but that (or a similar update) has not yet been
> merged into 2.0.1.

I don't think we're ready to turn on C++11 yet.

We are about to merge in the grammar fixes. By 2.1 at
least. We're working on some critical issues first, like
fixing the sd() gradients.

> As I said, my Python/Django days are a while ago, but I'm pretty sure if the stanc would be build with -O0 (like O_STANC
> = 0 in the vanilla makefile of the stan distribution) this will fix the issue.

Agreed.

- Bob

Hi,

For those who want to play around with flags and try to get things working on OS
X Mavericks, it's easy. Check out the development branch on github: git clone
https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan

and add / subtract flags in these two lines:

setup.py
102:extra_compile_args = ['-O3', '-ftemplate-depth-256']

pystan/model.py
247: extra_compile_args = ['-O3', '-ftemplate-depth-256']

then do a `python setup.py install` (remembering to change out of the source
directory when/if it finishes compiling)

Best,

-a

I had indeed seen that local reference return warning, but ignored it. I hadn't noticed that as a side effect of reinstalling MacPorts on Mavericks, my default compiler had reverted to clang!

If I switch to gcc 4.8 from MacPorts (which it had installed anyway to build SciPy), it seems to work fine. Nice job recognizing the symptoms of a miscompilation! Rob, did you mean that your fix requires C++11 extensions, or that your fix is required in order to later enable C++11 extensions?

You have to switch both the initial pystan compilation and the model building, so either do:

$ CC=gcc-mp-4.8 python setup.py install
$ CC=gcc-mp-4.8 ipython

or just

$ export CC=gcc-mp-4.8
$ python setup.py install
...

I haven't tried clang with lower optimization yet, though I may try that soon because -O3 on both compilers is quite slow to compile.

The gcc-4.8 compilation is unfortunately chatty; it dumps a ton of undefined-local-typedefs warnings from Boost, like the following:

Hi Ken,

Glad you've got it working. Trying the clang path creates all kind of other problems which maybe are related to the Python/Mavericks issues Allen was referring to. If someone is interested in the details, just shoot me an email.

The fix I was referring to really does 2 things, 1) it enables compilation of the stan compiler using clang++ at higher levels of optimization and 2) it  makes it possible to compile stan using the c++11 extensions. Neither of these are a real benefit to Stan today, so I fully agree with Bob to be really careful when to include such a fix in Stan. 

I did it because I am developing a library in C++ and wanted to make sure I could use c++11 extensions and not have to worry about compatibility with R itself and other installed R packages based on C++.

Rob J. Goedman
goe...@icloud.com

You have to switch both the initial pystan compilation and the model building, so either do:

Hi,

For those who want to play around with flags and try to get things working on OS
X Mavericks, it's easy. Check out the development branch on github: git clone
https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan

and add / subtract flags in these two lines:

setup.py
102:extra_compile_args = ['-O3', '-ftemplate-depth-256']

pystan/model.py
247:        extra_compile_args = ['-O3', '-ftemplate-depth-256']

then do a `python setup.py install` (remembering to change out of the source
directory when/if it finishes compiling)

Best,

-a
